definition: RTOs/ISOs typically run a day-ahead auction that prices the next day's power in one-hour blocks based on forecasted load, followed by a real-time auction that continuously reconciles actual demand against that forecast in five-minute increments.
core_idea: The day-ahead auction, usually finalized in the early afternoon before delivery, lets generators plan fuel and operations around a load forecast, while the real-time auction runs throughout the delivery day balancing actual versus forecast demand and favors plants capable of starting and stopping quickly.
key_points: Day-ahead auction prices the next day's power in one-hour increments, typically completed in the early afternoon before delivery.
Day-ahead prices are based on a predicted (forecast) load, not actual demand.
Real-time auction runs continuously through the delivery day, typically in five-minute increments, balancing actual demand against the day-ahead forecast.
A plant not selected in the day-ahead auction can still bid into the real-time auction.
Real-time participation requires the ability to start and stop quickly, which not every plant can do.
Only power plants participate directly in these auctions, but the resulting price affects every market participant.
relationships: Both auctions use the same marginal-price/clearing-price mechanic described for deregulated market auctions
trading_implications: Fast-ramping or flexible generation has an advantage bidding into the real-time auction when not cleared day-ahead.
The existence of two sequential auctions (forecast-based day-ahead, actuals-based real-time) is the structural basis for day-ahead vs. real-time price spreads.
caveats: The real-time auction is not a single event — it runs continuously in five-minute increments throughout the delivery day, unlike the one-time day-ahead auction.
